historical_record.description: The library building was under construction on the southeast corner of McCoppin Square.

The Parkside branch of the San Francisco Public Library opened, designed by Appleton and Wolfard with landscaping by Lawrence Halprin and built to look less like an institution than a house: an open plan around a copper-hooded fireplace and reading lounge, an outdoor patio, Eames and Herman Miller furniture. The pair went on to design the Marina, Ortega, Merced, North Beach, Eureka, Western Addition and Excelsior branches between 1953 and 1966.

The Parkside branch library, 1951, by Appleton & Wolfard — the first of the eight branch libraries the firm designed, and the prototype for the casual, inviting Midcentury Modern library that broke with the Carnegie branches before it.

The Parkside branch opened as the nineteenth branch of the San Francisco Public Library, the first of eight Midcentury Modern branches Appleton & Wolfard designed in collaboration with City Librarian Laurence Clarke.
The San Francisco Chronicle hailed the new building as the finest branch library in the country.
Architect and Engineer put the library on its cover and likened it to a swank country club or a luxurious modern house.
The city Planning Department named the Parkside branch the pilot project and proving ground for its whole program of public library building.
The Parkside branch had the highest circulation of the 21 city library branches.
Possibly the Park and Shop Market, later Andronico’s Market, designed by architect Robert B. Marquis.
The library hosted "Movies and Talkies," pairing boxing memorabilia and classic fight films with talks by a boxing champion.
The library hosted a "Multicultural Festival" with a talk for children.

A $4.7 million renovation and expansion began under the Branch Library Improvement Program, designed by Thomas Hacker Architects with an associate firm: the interior was gutted, a one-story addition of about 1,000 square feet was built at the east end, all windows were replaced, new openings were cut onto the rear terrace, and seismic, accessibility and systems upgrades were made.
The Historic Preservation Commission directed that landmark initiation for the library be calendared once the branch library improvement program was finished; no such hearing followed.

As part of the renovation, the original red brick fireplace and copper hood, the exposed brick wall and built-in bench, and the boxed-inset ceiling of the former reading room were restored, and the rear terrace was repaired.
The library reopened after renovation, the fifteenth project completed under the Branch Library Improvement Program; the work later earned LEED Silver certification.
The Board of Supervisors adopted a resolution initiating landmark designation of the Parkside Branch Library.
The Historic Preservation Commission held a hearing and recommended the library for landmark designation.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 310, Parkside Branch Library.
